raw_response:
I have farmed these 15 mu in Quzhou for 45 years. I know every patch of soil, and at 67 I do not waste money on things that do not pay back. My household has three mouths to feed, so wheat and maize must come first—they are our staple grains and the safest crops on the North China Plain. I will keep 9 mu in the wheat-maize rotation. The wheat went into the ground last autumn, and now in spring it needs a top-dressing of nitrogen and one irrigation at jointing. After we cut the wheat in early June, I will sow hybrid maize directly into the stubble without ploughing. No-tillage saves labor, keeps moisture, and gives me enough time to get the summer crop in before the rains stop. 

For cash, I rely on cotton and peanut. Cotton prices have been decent, and 3 mu will give us spending money for the year, but I must spray for bollworm. Peanut is easier on the body and the oil is good for our own table too; I will plant 2 mu. Both fields will get a pass with the rotary tiller in late April before sowing improved seeds. 

I always keep about 1 mu of mungbean. My family likes mungbean soup in the hot summer, it fixes some nitrogen back into the soil, and I can save the seed for next year. I will till that small plot in June and plant the saved traditional seed. 

I have a well, so I can irrigate when the dry spells come, but pumping costs electricity. Wheat gets three waters—jointing and grain-filling are the most important. Maize gets two, cotton three, peanut two, and mungbean only needs one because it tolerates dryness. For fertilizer, I put more nitrogen on the grain crops and less on the legumes. Pesticides are kept to a minimum except on cotton, which needs four sprays to keep the worms off.
